newsitem.title: UK: Irish govt disappointed over parade handling.
newsitem.headline: Irish govt disappointed over parade handling.

text.p: An Anglo-Irish attempt to find a negotiated settlement for Northern Ireland hit fresh problems on Sunday when the holding of an Orange Order parade angered the new Dublin government and drew scorn from Irish nationalists.

Irish Prime Minister Bertie Ahern's newly-elected government expressed "deep disappointment" at Britain's decision to allow the Protestant parade along Portadown's Catholic Garvaghy Road over the objections of the government and local residents.
Ahern's government, in power since June 26, said in a statement that it had "left the British government in no doubt about our serious concern" over the way the parade was handled.

Officials said Britain's Prime Minister Tony Blair, in power since May 1 elections, told Ahern of the decision to allow the parade personally in one of only a handful of contacts the two men have had since they came to office.

Martin McGuinness, a key leader of the IRA guerrillas' political wing, Sinn Fein, said he was disgusted by the decision to allow the parade and said Britain's new government had "failed its first test miserably".

The parade was held weeks after Blair reopened lines of contact with Sinn Fein to try to persuade its Irish Republican Army (IRA) backers to end their 28-year war against British rule to get Sinn Fein invited to the peace talks.

It is barred from the negotiations because of IRA violence and the province's pro-British Unionist leaders say it cannot be admitted until it has proved its democratic credentials by agreeing to a phased surrender of its weapons.
The Orange Order, whose members include many of Northern Ireland's Protestant political elite, refused to talk to the Garvaghy Road residents, accusing them of being tools of the IRA.
David Trimble, head of the Ulster Unionist Party, rejected allegations that the Order, of which he is a member, had failed to take Catholic objections into account.
"Their (the Orange Order's) attitude is that they are not going to be driven out of what is part of their own town," he told reporters in mainly Protestant Portadown.

Lines of contact between Sinn Fein and the two governments were closed after the IRA murdered two policemen in Lurgan last month but British and Irish officials had hoped that the annual Protestant "marching season" would pass off in relative peace and be greeted by a new IRA truce.
Hours after the parade a hooded gunman assumed to be from an Irish republican guerrilla faction fired at police but missed before melting into a maze of Catholic back streets in Belfast.
The scene, captured on television cameras, underlined the failure of attempts to date to get the IRA to call a new truce and negotiate a handover of its arsenal of bombs and weapons.

The IRA casts itself as a defender of the 40 percent Catholic minority against the Protestant majority. Both governments say its violence is mindless and futile and will do nothing to help reach a negotiated settlement.

Dublin's carefully-worded statement mixed anger at the way the parade was allowed despite Catholic objections with determination that the two governments should continue a three-year initiative to reconcile the two communities.
It called on Northern Ireland's polarised 1.5 million people not to react violently "but in the difficult period ahead all concerned on both sides must act with dignity and restraint," it said.
"Above all, we must not allow this decision to deflect us from the search for peace," said the statement.
